WA:
Washington packs two different kinds of camping into one state. West of the Cascades, campgrounds sit in rainforest and along Puget Sound, including the Cascadia Marine Trail: a chain of small sites you reach by kayak or small boat, not by van. East of the crest it gets drier, with national forest campgrounds up the valleys around Leavenworth, Cle Elum and Winthrop, and lakeside spots through the Okanogan and the Columbia Basin.

Many of the listings below are national forest campgrounds matched to official records. Private RV parks cluster along the coast and near towns like Port Angeles, Birch Bay and Grand Coulee. A good number are backcountry camps on trails in the Olympics and North Cascades: worth knowing about, but you carry your bed in rather than park it. Passes and forest roads close for snow, so check seasonal openings before you drive up.
TX:
Most of what's listed in Texas is RV parks, close to 800 of them, and they're spread wherever people work or vacation. Odessa and Midland have the biggest cluster, a lot of them long-stay parks out in oil country. On the coast, Port Aransas has beach camping on permit and a strip of RV resorts. Bandera, in the Hill Country, and Bastrop, east of Austin, have smaller groups of their own.

The wilder end is out west. Around Study Butte, the listings are backcountry campsites in Big Bend, the kind you need a park permit for, and most of them are a hike or a rough road in. Summer out there is brutal, so most people go between October and April.
OR:
Oregon's list leans on the Cascades. The busiest areas are the lakes around Crescent Lake and Lemolo, the North Umpqua road east of Glide, and the Metolius River at Camp Sherman, where Forest Service campgrounds sit right on the water. Oakridge, La Pine and Government Camp fill in the rest of the range.

About 160 of the listings match official agency records, and another 30 or so are on BLM land. A lot of the high campgrounds open late and close early because of snow, so check before you count on one in spring or fall.
MN:
Minnesota's list is mostly about water. Near Ranier and Orr, a big share of the listings are island and shoreline sites on the border lakes, and plenty of them are reachable only by boat. If you're in a van, look at the RV parks in those towns instead and treat the water sites as a day trip.

Up the North Shore, Grand Marais and Lutsen have a mix of Superior National Forest campgrounds on inland lakes and small sites along the trails. Further west, around Cass Lake, there are a few more in the Chippewa National Forest. The camping season is short this far north, roughly May through September.
CO:
Colorado's biggest clusters sit on both sides of Rocky Mountain National Park. Estes Park has the park's main drive-in campgrounds, Moraine Park, Glacier Basin and Aspenglen, plus private parks in town. Grand Lake, on the west side, is mostly backcountry sites you hike to with a park permit.

Around 170 listings match official records, including Forest Service campgrounds near Red Feather Lakes, Gunnison and Bayfield. Out by Dinosaur, the listings are river camps along the Green and Yampa, for float trips rather than road trips. Many of the high campgrounds don't open until June.
MI:
Most of Michigan's listings are in the Upper Peninsula. Munising, at Pictured Rocks, has the biggest group, from backcountry sites along the lakeshore and Hiawatha National Forest campgrounds to private parks in town. Grand Marais, Newberry and Manistique have a run of small state forest campgrounds on lakes and rivers, often with just a handful of sites each.

In the Lower Peninsula, Baldwin and Mio sit in the Huron-Manistee National Forest, and private RV parks make up most of the rest. St. Ignace is the easy stop at the bridge. Expect bugs in June and full campgrounds on summer weekends.
UT:
Moab has the most listings in Utah. A lot of them are small BLM campgrounds strung along the Colorado River just outside town, and they fill fast in spring and fall. Springdale, at the edge of Zion, is the other busy one.

For something quieter, look at Hanksville and the San Rafael Swell, where the listings include Temple Mountain and campgrounds up in the Henry Mountains. Flaming Gorge in the northeast corner has Forest Service campgrounds around the reservoir. About 140 listings match official records. Summer in the desert is hot, so the high campgrounds are where people go from June to August.
AK:
Alaska's list looks different from other states. Almost half of it is official agency records, and a lot of those are Forest Service public-use cabins in the Tongass around Petersburg, Sitka and Wrangell. You reserve them ahead and most are reached by boat or floatplane, not by road.

If you're driving, the listings near Seward and Cooper Landing on the Kenai, and Whittier on Prince William Sound, are the ones you can pull into. Around Paxson, the sites are small river camps, better suited to a float trip than a vehicle. Distances are long and services are thin between towns, so plan fuel and water with that in mind.
WY:
Most of Wyoming's listings are inside or right next to Yellowstone and Grand Teton. The ones near West Yellowstone, Silver Gate, Mammoth and the Bechler corner by Warm River are mostly backcountry campsites in Yellowstone, and the ones near Kelly are the same in Grand Teton. You need a backcountry permit for those, and you walk or paddle in.

For drive-in camping, look at the private parks in the gateway towns and around Cody. Around 120 listings match official records. The parks' road campgrounds book up months ahead in summer, and the high country holds snow into June.
PA:
Pennsylvania's listings are mostly private, paid campgrounds spread across the state. The biggest cluster is around Fayetteville and Mont Alto in Michaux State Forest, where there are numbered primitive sites alongside the private campgrounds near Gettysburg.

Up in the northwest, Marienville sits in the Allegheny National Forest, with Forest Service recreation areas and an equestrian campground among the listings. Lancaster County, around Conestoga, has private campgrounds within reach of the farm country. Only a handful of listings are agency records, so it's worth checking hours and seasons before you go.
